gap: No result ChatGPT got states watt-hours per pound, dollars per watt of AC output or dollars per measured usable Wh for the under-$400 1 kWh stations: the BLUETTI Elite 100 mini carries 42.6 Wh/lb against 32.7 for the DJI Power 1000 V2 and 35.3 for the Pecron E1000LFP, while the DJI costs $0.15 per continuous watt against the mini's $0.54.
standout_why: Compared against PopSci's Black Friday deals page (the cited one), OutletPicks' 1,000–1,299 Wh page, Backup Power Hub and JuiceBench. PopSci gives price, Wh and some weights but no ratio of any kind, and does not mention the Pecron, DJI, ALLPOWERS or OUPES units. OutletPicks and Backup Power Hub give dollars per rated Wh only ($0.37 DJI, $0.38 mini); OutletPicks lists no weights. Backup Power Hub gives a generic runtime formula (Wh × 0.85 ÷ load) with no per-unit figure. JuiceBench prices nothing in this class under $450. None divides capacity by weight, price by output watts, or price by a reviewer-measured Wh, and none has a kettle count. Rivals already have the $/rated-Wh part, so this is not a 3.
decides: It splits the line the way the desk research placed it, with numbers. On rated $/Wh the three are within 2 cents ($0.37–0.39), so that figure cannot decide. Dollars per output watt does: at near-identical prices the DJI gives 2,600 W against the mini's 700 W, so the DJI wins general use if its $379.99 holds on DJI's own store (I could only read it on two trackers). The Elite 100 mini, which we link, honestly wins the carry-weight segment: 30% more Wh per lb than the DJI, 21% more than the Pecron. It cannot run the 1,074 W kettle The Gadgeteer ran about six times per charge on the Pecron. ChatGPT's pick, the Pecron, leads on neither ratio. One caution for the page: OutletPicks lists off-brand 1,024–1,042 Wh units at $299.99–$358.69 that meet the question's line and undercut all of these on $/Wh.

findings.label: Energy per pound (rated)
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 100 mini Portable Power Station | 1,004Wh 700W
findings.note: 1,004.8 Wh ÷ 23.6 lb = 42.6 Wh/lb. Both inputs are BLUETTI's own: 'Packs 1,004.8Wh of capacity', 'weighs just 23.6 lb'.

findings.label: Price per rated Wh, store price
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 100 mini Portable Power Station | 1,004Wh 700W
findings.note: $379.00 ÷ 1,004.8 Wh = $0.377. Store price $379.00 (was $429.00), in stock, '2–5 Business Days Delivery'; storecheck.py and the page agree. At the brief's cart-tested link price: $360.05 ÷ 1,004.8 = $0.358.

findings.label: Price per continuous AC watt
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 100 mini Portable Power Station | 1,004Wh 700W
findings.note: $379.00 ÷ 700 W = $0.541. BLUETTI: 'Total output not to exceed 700W.' The page text I read gave no Power Lifting figure.

findings.label: Wall refill rate to 80%
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 100 mini Portable Power Station | 1,004Wh 700W
findings.note: 0.80 × 1,004.8 Wh = 803.8 Wh in 1.5 h = 536 Wh/h. BLUETTI: '80% in 90 minutes at home', 700 W AC input. Charge losses ignored.

findings.label: Solar refill at the unit's maximum solar input
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 100 mini Portable Power Station | 1,004Wh 700W
findings.note: 1,004.8 Wh ÷ 350 W = 2.87 h. BLUETTI: 'up to 350W solar'. Assumes the full 350 W arrives the whole time, which real panels do not deliver. Same page: 10 ms UPS, 6,000+ cycles.

findings.label: Usable capacity, measured by a named reviewer
findings.note: GearLab (Kenji Mowrey, 2026-07-23) measured 880 Wh; 880 ÷ 1,024 = 85.9%. The page does not state the test load.

findings.label: Energy per pound
findings.value: 32.5 Wh/lb rated; 27.9 Wh/lb on measured output
findings.note: 1,024 Wh ÷ 31.5 lb = 32.5; 880 Wh ÷ 31.5 lb = 27.9. The 31.5 lb is GearLab's measured weight. With The Solar Lab's listed 31.3 lb: 1,024 ÷ 31.3 = 32.7.

findings.label: Minutes of a 1,500 W heater or kettle per charge
findings.note: 880 Wh ÷ 1,500 W = 0.587 h = 35 min. Uses GearLab's measured 880 Wh, whose test load is unstated; efficiency at 1,500 W may differ.

findings.label: Wall refill rate, measured
findings.value: 1,041 Wh per hour; full in 59 minutes
findings.note: GearLab's own figures: 'Taking just 59 minutes to reach a full charge'. Against the mini's 536 Wh/h to 80%: 1,041 ÷ 536 = 1.9 times the rate.

findings.label: Self-consumption over a day
findings.value: about 432 Wh in 24 hours, 42% of the rated capacity
findings.source_title: DJI Power 1000 V2 portable power station review | The Solar Lab
findings.note: 18 W × 24 h = 432 Wh; 432 ÷ 1,024 = 42%. The Solar Lab reports about 18 W of draw while powered on, without saying clearly whether the AC inverter was on, so treat as indicative. Same review: 82% efficiency, 2,600 W inverter, 31.3 lb listed.

findings.label: Price per Wh and per continuous watt, at the tracker-reported price
findings.value: $0.371 per rated Wh; $0.432 per measured Wh; $0.146 per W
findings.source_title: Black Friday Power Station & Solar Generator Deals 2026 | Backup Power Hub
findings.note: $379.99 ÷ 1,024 = $0.371; $379.99 ÷ 880 (GearLab) = $0.432; $379.99 ÷ 2,600 W = $0.146. The $379.99 is Backup Power Hub's reading of djiusa.com (page dated 2026-11-25); OutletPicks showed the same $379.99 on 2026-11-27. I did not read it on DJI's store: re-read before publishing.

findings.label: Energy per pound (rated)
findings.source_title: Pecron E1000LFP portable power station review | The Gadgeteer
findings.note: 1,024 Wh ÷ 29 lb = 35.3. The Gadgeteer (James Cook, 2025-02-14) reproduces Pecron's spec sheet: 'Capacity: 1024Wh', 'Weight : 29lbs(13.5Kg)', rated 1,800 W, peak 3,000 W. Pecron's own page returned 429.

findings.label: Kettle heating cycles per charge
findings.source_title: Pecron E1000LFP portable power station review | The Gadgeteer
findings.note: 100% ÷ 16% per cycle = 6.25. James Cook measured a 1,074 W peak draw and about 16% of the battery for one whole heating cycle; he does not give the water volume. That kettle exceeds the Elite 100 mini's 700 W limit.

findings.label: Wall and solar refill, from the spec sheet
findings.value: about 788 Wh per hour on AC; 1.7 hours at maximum solar input
findings.source_title: Pecron E1000LFP portable power station review | The Gadgeteer
findings.note: 1,024 Wh ÷ 1.3 h = 788 Wh/h (spec sheet: 'AC Input: 100V~120V/ 1000W', 'Charging Time: 1.3 Hours'); 1,024 Wh ÷ 600 W = 1.71 h best case (spec sheet: XT60, 11–60 V, 600 W max). Cook's own run: 50% to full in about half an hour.

findings.label: What the rival pages already state
findings.note: OutletPicks ranks 'by cost per Wh': DJI Power 1000 V2 $379.99, $0.37; BLUETTI Elite 100 mini $379.99, $0.38. No weights, runtimes or usable-Wh figures. PopSci's deals page (https://www.popsci.com/gear/black-friday-portable-power-station-deals/, read the same day) has the mini at $379.99 on Amazon and 23.6 lb, with no ratios.

findings.label: Cheaper off-brand units that also meet 1,000 Wh under $400
findings.note: As listed: BALDR 1,042 Wh $299.99; Staryline 1,024 Wh $299.99–$339.99; CTOLITY AP1000 1,024 Wh / 1,800 W $339.99; Arkpax 1,024 Wh $358.69. Wattages are listing-title figures, some of them peak. The page must say why these are in or out. Just outside the line on the same page: Grecell 999 Wh $246.99 (under 1,000 Wh), EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic $438.90 and OUPES Mega 1 Lite $439.00 (over $400).

unsourced: Pecron E1000LFP price today: pecron.com returned 403 to storecheck and 429 to fetches, and FactoryPure (the retailer ChatGPT showed at $399.00) returned 429 and 403. Off Grid Stores also returned 403. If $399.00 is confirmed, the arithmetic is $399 ÷ 1,024 Wh = $0.390/Wh and $399 ÷ 1,800 W = $0.222/W.

DJI Power 1000 V2 price, stock notice and spec table on DJI's own US store: store.dji.com redirected to an account page and dji.com/power-1000-v2/specs redirected to a 404. The Amazon check was not run. The $379.99 above comes from two tracker pages only.

ALLPOWERS P1800 weight, recharge time and store price read today: allpowers.com resolved to a corporate site with no product data, and iallpowers.com returned 403 and 429. So no Wh/lb for the P1800 (the desk note's 28.7 lb is unverified). From the brief's cart-tested prices only: $395.10 ÷ 1,024 Wh = $0.386/Wh and $395.10 ÷ 1,800 W = $0.220/W with the code; $439.00 ÷ 1,024 = $0.429/Wh without.
A named reviewer's measured usable Wh for the BLUETTI Elite 100 mini, the Pecron E1000LFP and the ALLPOWERS P1800: I had no calls left to look, so dollars per usable Wh is given for the DJI only.

Standby or idle draw for the Elite 100 mini, the Pecron and the P1800: BLUETTI's product page text does not state one, and The Gadgeteer's review has none. The 24-hour overhead figure therefore exists for the DJI only.
A fridge maker's average running watts, needed for a fridge-hours-per-charge line: not looked up.
OUPES Mega 1 (non-Lite) price: oupes.com returned 403. OutletPicks shows only the Mega 1 Lite at $439.00, which is over the line.
